questions.title: When can a court decide fair use on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion instead of waiting for summary judgment?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural posture here. Fair use is an affirmative defense, so I thought defendants usually have to prove it later in the case after discovery. But the Second Circuit says fair use can be so clearly established by the complaint that dismissal at the pleading stage is proper. What exactly has to be in the complaint or incorporated materials for that to happen? Is the idea that the court can compare the original videos and the TV segment itself without resolving factual disputes?

questions.title: How can a use be 'transformative' if the alleged infringer caused the original work to be created?
questions.question_body: Santos argued that Kimmel was basically the 'designer' of the original purpose of the Cameo videos because he submitted the requests under fake names and prompted Santos to make the videos in the first place. The court still says the later broadcast use was transformative because a reasonable observer would see the original videos as positive messages, while the TV segment used them to comment on Santos's willingness to say absurd things for money. If the defendant sets up the facts so that the original work exists, why doesn't that collapse the distinction between the original purpose and the secondary use?

questions.title: After Harper & Row, does bad faith or deception still matter in a fair use analysis?
questions.question_body: The opinion says Santos claimed Kimmel's false representations and use of fictitious names showed bad faith, which should defeat fair use. The court responds that the Supreme Court has since distanced itself from Harper & Row's statement that fair use presupposes good faith and fair dealing. I'm having trouble understanding the current law here. Does bad faith still count as part of factor one, or is it mostly irrelevant unless it shows market substitution or some other concrete harm?

questions.title: Why didn't reputational or commercial damage from mockery count as market harm under factor four?
questions.question_body: The court says the fourth fair use factor asks whether the secondary work usurps the market for the original by acting as a competing substitute, not whether it damages the original through parody or criticism. But if Kimmel's segment makes people less likely to buy Santos Cameos in the future, isn't that still economic harm flowing from the use? I'm confused why that kind of lost demand is not considered market harm under copyright law.

questions.title: Why did the court rely on the copyright registrations to say the videos were published the same day they were created?
questions.question_body: In discussing the other fair use factors, the court says the copyright registrations establish that the videos were published on the same day they were created, and it takes judicial notice of the Copyright Office records. How does that matter for the fair use analysis? Is the unpublished/published distinction still important under factor two, and can a court really treat those registration facts as settled on a motion to dismiss?

questions.title: Why could the Second Circuit avoid the Copyright Act preemption issue and just affirm on state-law pleading grounds?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed the contract claims as preempted, but the Second Circuit says it 'need not resolve this issue' because the claims fail under state law anyway. Is that just a general appellate rule that a court can affirm on any ground supported by the record? Or is there some reason preemption should have been decided first? I'm trying to understand the sequencing here.

questions.title: Can a Cameo creator sue a customer for breaching the platform's Terms of Service as a third-party beneficiary?
questions.question_body: For the express contract claim, Santos relied on the Cameo Terms of Service that users like Kimmel agreed to, but the court says Santos was not a party to that contract and was not an intended third-party beneficiary under Illinois law. What would Santos have needed to point to in the Terms of Service to get around the strong presumption against third-party enforcement? The court mentions that other provisions expressly gave rights to third parties. Is that what doomed this claim?

questions.title: What was missing from Santos's implied contract and fraudulent inducement claims under New York law?
questions.question_body: I'm also confused about the state-law merits rulings. For implied-in-fact contract, the court says Santos did not plead the essential terms or a meeting of the minds that Kimmel would follow the Terms of Service. What sort of allegations would normally be enough to show an implied agreement in this kind of online transaction? And for fraudulent inducement, why wasn't being tricked into making the videos enough to show damages if New York requires an 'out-of-pocket loss'?
